slides.title: What is Biology?
content: Biology is the scientific study of life or living things.
Derived from Greek: 'bios' (life) + 'logos' (study).
Biology is a science of inquiry and observation.

slides.title: Characteristics of Living Things
content: Living things are composed of one or more cells.
They can grow, reproduce, and transmit genetic information.
They need energy to accomplish work.
They maintain homeostasis (relatively constant internal conditions).
They are capable of evolutionary adaptation to the environment.

slides.title: What is a Scientific Study?
content: Biologists study living things using the scientific method.
The process involves asking questions, suggesting possible answers, and testing their validity.
Study can be direct (using sense organs) or indirect (using tools like microscopes).

slides.title: Biology's Relationship with Other Sciences
content: Biology merges information and tools from all natural sciences.
Chemistry: Studies elements, chemical bonding, molecules, acids, bases in living organisms.
Physics: Explains energy conversion, like photosynthesis (radiant energy to organic molecules).

slides.title: Applications of Biology in Daily Life
content: Wine-making, brewing, baking, and cheese production depend on fermentation by yeasts and bacteria.
Antibiotics (e.g., penicillin) are produced by mould fungi or bacteria.
Production of industrial chemicals like citric acid uses bacteria or fungi.
Sewage disposal depends on bacteria in filter beds.

slides.title: Importance of Studying Biology
content: Helps understand how living things work and interact with the environment.
Biology touches everyday life: disease treatment, ecosystem function, genetics, forensics.
Helps evaluate environmental issues like global warming.
Used in treating diseases like AIDS, tuberculosis, and cancer.

slides.title: Steps of the Scientific Method
content: 1. Observation: Careful study of a problem.
2. Asking Questions: Formulating inquiries based on observations.
3. Forming a Hypothesis: Proposing a possible explanation that is testable.
4. Testing the Hypothesis: Conducting experiments.
5. Making Conclusions: Determining if data supports or rejects the hypothesis.
6. Communicating Findings: Sharing results via scientific journals.

slides.title: Hypothesis and Experimentation
content: A hypothesis is a proposed scientific explanation for a set of questions.
It must be testable through experimentation.
Experiments must be repeatable to be scientifically valid.
If a hypothesis is not supported, a new hypothesis can be proposed.

slides.title: Activity: Effect of Temperature on Germination
content: Objective: Determine the importance of temperature for seed germination.
Materials: Bean seeds, different temperature environments.
Groups: Room temperature, cold place (refrigerator), hot place (kitchen).
Measure: Time of germination and length of seedlings.
Create: Bar graph with time on X-axis and length on Y-axis.
Interpret and report results.

slides.title: Laboratory Tools: Observation and Magnification
content: Hand Lens: A convex lens providing enlarged images of objects.
Microscope: The most important tool for observing small objects, providing magnification and resolution.

slides.title: Laboratory Tools: Culturing and Sterilization
content: Autoclave: Sterilizes equipment and media with high-pressure steam.
Incubator: Maintains optimal temperature for microorganism growth.
Petri Dishes: Used with gelling media like agar for culturing.
Culture Tubes: Used for growing microorganisms in solid or liquid media.
Flasks: Used for large-volume broth cultures.

slides.title: Laboratory Tools: Measuring and Handling
content: Balance: Weighs specimens and ingredients.
Dropper: Controls addition of liquids.
Tongs: Handles hot objects.
Dissecting Kit: Contains tools for dissection (scalpel, forceps, scissors).
Dissecting Pan: Holds specimens during dissection.
Crucible: Withstands high temperatures for melting substances.
Beaker: Holds or heats liquids.
Hot Plate: Heats solutions.
pH Meter: Measures acidity/basicity.
Thermometer: Measures temperature.
Forceps: Holds or picks up small objects.
Spatula: Mixes, stirs, or scrapes substances.
Wash Bottles: Rinse laboratory materials.

slides.title: Field Tools
content: Insect Net: Used for collecting insects; made of cloth or fine mesh.
Fishing Net: Used for capturing fish; often in a grid-like structure.

slides.title: Introduction to the Light Microscope
content: A light microscope uses a beam of light to view specimens.
Compound light microscope has two or more glass lenses.
Total magnification = Magnification of eyepiece × Magnification of objective lens.
Example: 10x eyepiece × 40x objective = 400x total magnification.

slides.title: Parts and Functions: Structural Parts
content: Arm: Supports the microscope; used for carrying.
Base: The bottom support of the microscope.
Stage: Platform where the specimen is placed for viewing.
Stage Clips: Hold the slide in place on the stage.
Aperture: Hole on the stage for light to pass through.
Body Tube: Connects the eyepiece to the objective lenses.

slides.title: Parts and Functions: Optical Parts
content: Eyepiece (Ocular): Top part used to look through (typically 10x magnification).
Objective Lenses: Main magnifying lenses (4x, 10x, 40x, 100x).
Nose Piece: Rotating mechanism holding objective lenses.
Adjustment Knobs: Coarse focus (brings specimen into general focus) and fine focus (sharpens image).

slides.title: Parts and Functions: Light System
content: Microscopic Illuminator: The light source at the base of the microscope.
Condenser: Lenses below the stage that focus light onto the specimen.
Diaphragm (Iris): Controls the amount of light reaching the specimen.

slides.title: Handling and Using a Light Microscope
content: Carry with one hand on the arm and the other supporting the base.
Always start with the lowest power objective (4x).
Focus with coarse adjustment first, then use fine adjustment.
Never touch lenses with fingers; clean with lens paper and alcohol.
Use immersion oil only with the 100x objective.
Always lower the stage and remove the slide when finished.
Before storing, place the 4x objective over the stage and lower the stage completely.

slides.title: Importance of Laboratory Safety
content: Safety is the condition of being protected from harm or danger.
It involves recognizing and controlling hazards.
Working carefully, addressing problems early, and maintaining constant safety awareness.

slides.title: General Safety Rules (Part 1)
content: Follow the instructions: Read and listen to all procedures carefully.
Know safety equipment: Know the location of fire extinguisher, first-aid kit, and eyewash.
Dress for the lab: Wear safety goggles, lab coat, gloves, long pants, and closed-toe shoes.
Never eat or drink in the laboratory.

slides.title: General Safety Rules (Part 2)
content: Never taste or sniff chemicals: Label containers and read before use.
Act responsibly: Do not randomly mix chemicals.
Clean the experiment area: Begin and end each session with a clean workspace.
Handle chemicals properly: Wear a respirator mask for toxic chemicals.

slides.title: General Safety Rules (Part 3)
content: Know what to do with accidents: Flood burns with cold water immediately.
Always prioritize safety and chemical hygiene.
Never leave containers open; all containers must be labeled.
Never use unlabelled chemicals.

slides.title: What Makes Something Living?
content: Living things exhibit a variety of shapes and forms.
They share a common set of characteristics.
These characteristics distinguish them from non-living matter.

slides.title: Key Characteristics of Life
content: Made of cells (unicellular or multicellular).
Require energy (autotrophs or heterotrophs).
Respond to stimuli.
Grow (increase in size and mass).
Reproduce (sexual or asexual).

slides.title: Additional Characteristics of Life
content: Excrete: Remove metabolic wastes like carbon dioxide.
Display ordered complexity: Atoms to molecules to organelles to cells to tissues, etc.
Maintain homeostasis: Regulate internal conditions (e.g., body temperature).
Possess adaptations that evolve over time.

slides.title: What is Taxonomy?
content: Taxonomy is the science of naming, identifying, and classifying organisms.
Classification groups organisms based on similarities.
Assumption: Greater physical similarity = closer biological relationship.

slides.title: History of Classification
content: Aristotle (384-322 BC) developed the first widely accepted classification system.
He used simple morphological characters (trees, shrubs, herbs).
He also divided animals into those with red blood and those without.

slides.title: Linnaean Taxonomic Hierarchy
content: Developed by Carolus Linnaeus (1707-1778), the 'father of taxonomy'.
He introduced a ranked hierarchy of classification.
The ranks are: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.
Each level is called a taxon (plural: taxa).

slides.title: The Three Domains of Life
content: Bacteria: Prokaryotic cells, common bacteria.
Archaea: Prokaryotic cells, often inhabit extreme environments.
Eukarya: Eukaryotic cells (protists, fungi, plants, animals).

slides.title: Why is Classification Important?
content: Identifies harmful and beneficial organisms.
Reduces time and energy to study organisms.
Helps understand relationships between organisms (e.g., birds and dinosaurs).
Useful in agriculture, forestry, and medicine.
Helps discover new sources of lumber, foods, medicines, and energy.

slides.title: Example of Classification Application
content: A taxonomist may know a certain tree species has disinfectant properties.
This knowledge can lead to the discovery of similar useful substances in related plant species.
Expands the potential sources for important chemicals.

slides.title: Introduction to Binomial Nomenclature
content: Developed by Carl Linnaeus.
An internationally agreed system for naming organisms.
Each organism has a unique, two-part scientific name.
Avoids confusion caused by local and common names.

slides.title: Rules for Binomial Nomenclature
content: The first name is the Genus (capitalized).
The second name is the specific epithet (lowercase).
Example: Homo sapiens for humans.
Scientific names are underlined when handwritten or italicized when printed.
Example: Zea mays (maize).

slides.title: Ethiopia's Biodiversity
content: High biodiversity due to geographical location, topographical diversity, and diverse climatic features.
Hotspot for wild plant and animal species with high endemism.
Primary center of diversity for crops like noog (Guizotia abyssinica) and tef (Eragrostis tef).
Also diverse in barley, sorghum, durum wheat, finger millet, and various legumes.

slides.title: Common Ethiopian Animals
content: Elephant: Loxodonta africana.
Ethiopian Wolf: Canis simensis.
Gelada Baboon: Theropithecus gelada.
Lion: Panthera leo.
Walia Ibex: Capra walie.
Ostrich: Struthio camelus.
Watched Ibis: Bostrychia carunculata.

slides.title: Common Ethiopian Plants
content: Enset (False Banana): Ensete ventricosum.
Maize: Zea mays.
Noug: Guizotia abyssinica.
Tef: Eragrostis tef.
Wheat: Triticum aestivum.

slides.title: Dichotomous Keys
content: Used to identify unfamiliar organisms.
Made up of pairs of contrasting features.
'Dichotomous' means two branches.
Start with general characteristics and progress to more specific ones.
By making appropriate choices, the organism can be correctly identified.

slides.title: Why the Five-Kingdom System?
content: The two-kingdom (plant and animal) system was inadequate.
Many organisms did not fit into either category.
Whittaker (1969) proposed a five-kingdom system.
Criteria: cell structure, body organization, mode of nutrition, reproduction, and evolutionary relationships.

slides.title: The Five Kingdoms
content: 1. Kingdom Monera: Prokaryotic, unicellular.
2. Kingdom Protista: Eukaryotic, mostly unicellular, diverse.
3. Kingdom Fungi: Eukaryotic, heterotrophic, chitin cell wall.
4. Kingdom Plantae: Eukaryotic, autotrophic, cellulose cell wall.
5. Kingdom Animalia: Eukaryotic, heterotrophic, no cell wall.

slides.title: Why Viruses Are Not Included
content: Viruses are not considered living organisms.
They lack key characteristics of life: growth, development, respiration.
They are made of nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) in a protein coat.
They can only replicate inside a host cell.

slides.title: Characteristics of Monera
content: Simple prokaryotic, unicellular organisms.
Lack a well-defined nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.
Most have a rigid cell wall.
Various modes of nutrition: autotrophic (photosynthetic or chemosynthetic) or heterotrophic.
Known as decomposers and mineralizers in the biosphere.

slides.title: Eubacteria vs. Archaebacteria
content: Eubacteria (True Bacteria): Strong cell walls, found in most habitats, can be harmful or helpful.
Archaebacteria (Archaea): Different cell walls, live in extreme environments (swamps, hot springs, salt ponds), often chemosynthetic.

slides.title: Importance of Bacteria
content: Beneficial: Help with digestion, produce cheese and yogurt, fix nitrogen for plants.
Harmful: Cause diseases like tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) and chancroid.
Some bacteria release toxins that attack the host.

slides.title: Characteristics of Protists
content: The most diverse kingdom.
All are eukaryotes (have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles).
Can be unicellular or multicellular.
Some are microscopic, others are large.

slides.title: Types of Protists
content: Animal-like (Protozoans): Heterotrophs.
Plant-like (Algae): Photosynthetic autotrophs, basis of aquatic food chains, produce much of Earth's oxygen.
Fungus-like: Decomposers.

slides.title: Characteristics of Fungi
content: Eukaryotic organisms.
Can be unicellular (yeasts) or multicellular (moulds, mushrooms).
Made of long, slender thread-like structures called hyphae.
Cell wall made of chitin.
Heterotrophic (absorb nutrients after extracellular digestion).

slides.title: Types of Fungi
content: Saprophytes (Decomposers): Absorb nutrients from dead organic matter.
Parasites: Absorb nutrients from living hosts, causing disease (e.g., athlete's foot).
Mutualists: Benefit the host (e.g., lichens, mycorrhizae).

slides.title: Fungal Reproduction
content: Asexual: Fragmentation, fission, budding (yeast), or spore formation.
Sexual: Through the fusion of hyphae.
Spores are produced in distinct structures called fruiting bodies.

slides.title: Importance of Fungi
content: Decompose organic matter, recycling nutrients.
Used in baking and brewing (yeast).
Some cause diseases, but many are beneficial.

slides.title: Characteristics of Plants
content: Eukaryotic, multicellular autotrophs.
Make their own food through photosynthesis.
Contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll.
Have rigid cell walls made of cellulose.
Do not move from place to place.

slides.title: Major Plant Groups
content: Bryophytes: No vascular tissue (e.g., mosses, liverworts, hornworts).
Gymnosperms: Vascular, produce 'naked' seeds (e.g., conifers).
Angiosperms: Vascular, flowering plants, seeds in fruits.

slides.title: Angiosperms: Monocots and Dicots
content: Monocots: One seed leaf, parallel leaf veins (e.g., grasses, lilies).
Dicots: Two seed leaves, branching leaf veins (e.g., beans, roses).

slides.title: Characteristics of Animals
content: Multicellular, heterotrophic, eukaryotic organisms.
Ingest food and digest it internally.
Lack cell walls (held together by collagen).
Have specialized muscle and nerve cells.
Most reproduce sexually.

slides.title: Major Animal Groups
content: Invertebrates (No Backbone): Sponges, flatworms, roundworms, annelids, molluscs, arthropods.
Vertebrates (Backbone): Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.

Member of national and international professional organizations.
Served as Chair of the Biological Society of Ethiopia.
Secretary-General of the Association for the Taxonomic Study of Flora of Tropical Africa.
Director of Flora of Ethiopia and Gullele Botanical Garden.

slides.title: Definition of a Cell
content: The cell is the smallest and basic unit of living things.
All living things are composed of one or more cells.
Unicellular organisms: Composed of a single cell (e.g., Paramecium).
Multicellular organisms: Composed of many specialized cells (e.g., plants, animals, humans).

slides.title: Cells and Specialization
content: In multicellular organisms, cells are specialized for specific functions.
Muscle cells: Responsible for movement.
Nerve cells: Gather information and transmit signals.
Brain cells: Interpret messages and coordinate actions.
All activities of the body are results of cooperative work among cells.

slides.title: History of Cell Discovery
content: Robert Hooke (1665): First to observe cells and use the word 'cell' (viewed cork).
Anton van Leeuwenhoek (1674): First to observe living cells (protozoa and bacteria) using his microscopes.

slides.title: The Cell Theory
content: The cell theory is the unifying foundation of cell biology.
The three tenets of the cell theory:
1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the smallest unit of life.
3. Cells arise only by the division of a pre-existing cell.

slides.title: Contributors to Cell Theory
content: Matthias Schleiden (1838): Stated that plants are made of cells.
Theodor Schwann (1839): Stated that animals are made of cells.
Rudolf Virchow (1855): Stated that cells arise from pre-existing cells.

slides.title: Common Cell Structures
content: All cells share three common structural features:
1. Cell Membrane: Selectively permeable outer boundary.
2. Cytoplasm: Fluid-filled region containing organelles.
3. Nucleus: Control center containing DNA (except in prokaryotes).

slides.title: Cell Membrane and Nucleus
content: Cell Membrane: A thin, selectively permeable barrier that controls the movement of substances in and out of the cell.
Nucleus: The largest organelle, contains DNA, and controls all cell activities and cell division.

slides.title: Cytoplasm and Ribosomes
content: Cytoplasm: A thick fluid containing organelles; site of many chemical reactions (e.g., protein synthesis).
Ribosomes: Small structures found in large numbers; function is to synthesize proteins.

slides.title: Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)
content: A complex system of interconnected double membranes.
Rough ER: Studded with ribosomes; synthesizes and stores proteins.
Smooth ER: Lacks ribosomes; important for lipid synthesis.

slides.title: Golgi Apparatus and Vesicles
content: Golgi Apparatus: A smooth, concave membranous structure that modifies, packages, and distributes proteins and lipids.
Vesicles: Small sacs that store and transport materials within or outside the cell.

slides.title: Mitochondria and Lysosomes
content: Mitochondria: The 'powerhouse' of the cell; site of respiration and energy (ATP) production.
Lysosomes: Membrane-bound sacs of digestive enzymes that break down bacteria, unwanted substances, and damaged organelles.

slides.title: Vacuoles and Chloroplasts
content: Vacuoles: Storage sacs. Plant cells have a large central vacuole; animal cells have small vacuoles.
Chloroplasts: Site of photosynthesis in plant cells; contain the green pigment chlorophyll.

slides.title: Centrioles, Cilia, and Flagella
content: Centrioles: Involved in cell division (found in animal cells).
Cilia: Short, hair-like structures for locomotion or creating fluid currents.
Flagella: Long, thread-like structures for movement (e.g., sperm tail).

slides.title: Prokaryotic vs. Eukaryotic Cells
content: Prokaryotic Cells: No nucleus; no membrane-bound organelles; small and simple; always unicellular; have a cell wall.
Eukaryotic Cells: Have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; larger and more complex; usually multicellular.

slides.title: Key Differences
content: Organelles: Eukaryotes have them; Prokaryotes do not.
Ribosomes: Eukaryotes have larger ribosomes.
Chromosomes: Eukaryotic DNA is linear and associated with proteins; Prokaryotic DNA is circular and not associated with proteins.
Cell Wall: Present in prokaryotes and plant cells; absent in animal cells.
Cilia/Flagella: Present in some eukaryotes and prokaryotes.

slides.title: Similarities and Differences
content: Similarities: Both have a cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and Golgi apparatus.
Differences: Plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole.
Animal cells have centrioles and lysosomes (which are less common in plant cells).

slides.title: Preparing a Slide: Plant Cell
content: 1. Peel a thin layer of epidermal tissue from an onion.
2. Place it on a glass slide.
3. Add iodine solution (stain) to make structures visible.
4. Gently lower a coverslip at a 45° angle to avoid air bubbles.
5. View under a microscope, starting with the lowest power.

slides.title: Preparing a Slide: Animal Cell
content: 1. Rinse mouth to remove food particles.
2. Rub a cotton swab on the inside of the cheek.
3. Transfer the sample to a clean slide.
4. Add methylene blue dye (stain).
5. Gently lower a coverslip to avoid air bubbles.
6. View under the microscope.

slides.title: Cell Membrane Function
content: The cell membrane is selectively permeable.
It controls what enters and leaves the cell.
Substances can pass through via:
- Passive Transport (no energy needed): Diffusion and Osmosis.
- Active Transport (energy needed).

slides.title: Diffusion
content: The net movement of molecules from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration.
It is a passive process.
Examples: Oxygen diffusing into cells; the smell of perfume spreading.
Factors affecting diffusion: Concentration gradient, Temperature, Mass of molecule, Distance traveled, Surface area.

slides.title: Osmosis
content: The diffusion of water molecules across a semi-permeable membrane.
Water moves from a region of high water concentration (dilute solution) to low water concentration (concentrated solution).
It is a passive process.

slides.title: Osmosis and Solutions
content: Hypotonic: Lower solute concentration, higher water concentration (water moves into the cell).
Isotonic: Equal solute and water concentration (no net water movement).
Hypertonic: Higher solute concentration, lower water concentration (water moves out of the cell).

slides.title: Osmosis in Plant Cells
content: Hypotonic: Water enters, cell becomes turgid (rigid).
Isotonic: No net change.
Hypertonic: Water leaves, cell becomes flaccid and plasmolysed (shrunken).
Turgor pressure is important for keeping plants upright.

slides.title: Osmosis in Animal Cells
content: Animal cells lack a cell wall.
Hypotonic: Water enters, cell swells and may burst (hemolysis).
Hypertonic: Water leaves, cell shrinks.
Blood and tissue fluid are maintained at a concentration isotonic to cells.

slides.title: Active Transport
content: The movement of molecules from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration (against the concentration gradient).
Requires energy (from respiration).
Examples: Ion uptake by root hairs; glucose uptake by epithelial cells of villi.
Allows cells to maintain internal concentrations different from the environment.

slides.title: The Hierarchy of Life
content: Life is organized in a hierarchy from simple to complex.
The main levels are:
Atoms → Molecules → Organelles → Cells → Tissues → Organs → Organ Systems → Organisms → Populations → Communities → Ecosystems → Biosphere.

slides.title: Cellular and Organism Level
content: Cellular Level: Atoms form molecules, which make organelles within cells.
Organism Level: Similar cells form tissues; tissues form organs; organs form organ systems; organ systems work together to form an organism.

slides.title: Examples of Tissues, Organs, and Systems
content: Tissues: Groups of similar cells with a common function (e.g., muscle tissue, nerve tissue).
Organs: Structures made of different tissues that work together (e.g., heart, stomach, leaf).
Systems: Groups of organs that perform a major body function (e.g., digestive system, nervous system).

slides.title: Why Reproduction?
content: Reproduction is a unique characteristic of life.
It allows for the continuity of a species from generation to generation.
Two main modes: Asexual and Sexual reproduction.

slides.title: Asexual vs. Sexual Reproduction
content: Asexual: One parent, no gametes, genetically identical offspring.
Sexual: Two parents, gametes (sperm and egg), genetically different offspring.

slides.title: What is Asexual Reproduction?
content: Production of individuals without gametes.
Involves a single parent.
Results in offspring that are genetically identical to the parent.
Common in bacteria, protists, fungi, plants, and some invertebrates.
Absent in vertebrates.

slides.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
content: Advantages: No mate needed; all good traits passed on; rapid reproduction in favorable environments.
Disadvantages: Little genetic variation; adaption to change is unlikely; if parent is susceptible to disease, all offspring are; competition for resources.

slides.title: Fission
content: The organism divides into two (binary fission) or more (multiple fission) equal parts.
Common in bacteria, algae, and protozoa.
Binary fission: Parent divides into two equal parts.
Multiple fission: Nucleus divides repeatedly, producing many daughter cells.

slides.title: Fragmentation
content: The parent organism breaks into parts, each of which develops into a whole organism.
Common in fungi, algae, plants, and some animals (e.g., worms).
Example: Spirogyra (green algae) fragments into many filaments.

slides.title: Budding
content: A new organism develops as an outgrowth (bud) on the parent.
The two daughter cells are unequal in size.
Common in yeast (fungi) and Hydra (invertebrate).
The nucleus divides, and one daughter nucleus migrates into the bud.

slides.title: Vegetative Propagation (Natural)
content: A method of asexual reproduction in plants.
Structures with meristems (roots, stems, buds, leaves) give rise to new plants.
Stolons (Runners): Horizontal stems that grow along the soil surface (e.g., strawberry).
Rhizomes: Horizontal stems that grow underground (e.g., couch grass).
Corms: Round, fleshy underground stems (e.g., gladiolus).
Tubers: Swollen, modified stems that store starch (e.g., potato).
Bulbs: Modified stems with fleshy leaves (e.g., onion).

slides.title: Vegetative Propagation (Artificial)
content: Methods used by humans to create new plants.
Grafting: Joining a stem (scion) from one plant to the root (stock) of another.
Cutting: Placing a portion of a stem in soil or water to root.
Layering: Bending a stem to the ground and covering it with soil.

slides.title: Parthenogenesis
content: A form of asexual reproduction where an unfertilized egg develops into an adult organism.
Also known as 'virgin birth'.
Example: In honeybees, unfertilized eggs develop into male drones.

slides.title: Introduction to Sexual Reproduction
content: Involves two parent organisms.
Gametes (sex cells) are produced through meiosis.
The male gamete is sperm (small, motile).
The female gamete is the egg (larger, non-motile).
Fertilization is the union of sperm and egg.
This results in a single-celled zygote.

slides.title: Primary Sexual Characteristics
content: These are the reproductive organs present at birth.
Males: Penis, scrotum, and testicles.
Females: Vagina, uterus, and ovaries.

slides.title: Secondary Sexual Characteristics in Males
content: Develop during puberty due to the hormone testosterone.
Deepening of the voice.
Growth of facial, chest, and pubic hair.
Increased muscle mass and broadening of shoulders.
Increased growth of long bones in arms and legs.

slides.title: Secondary Sexual Characteristics in Females
content: Develop during puberty due to the hormone estrogen.
Breast development.
Widening of hips.
Deposition of fat in breasts, buttocks, and thighs.
Growth of underarm and pubic hair.
Beginning of the menstrual cycle.

slides.title: Psychological and Social Changes During Puberty
content: Young people undergo significant psychological and social changes.
There is a wide range of 'normal' development.
Body image can be a concern.
Early or late maturation can lead to psychological challenges.
Adolescence is the period between puberty and adulthood, marked by social learning and the achievement of economic and moral adulthood.

slides.title: Parts of the Male Reproductive System
content: Testes: Produce sperm and testosterone.
Scrotum: Sac holding the testes outside the body for temperature regulation.
Epididymis: Stores and matures sperm.
Vas Deferens: Tube that transports sperm from the epididymis to the urethra.
Seminal Vesicles: Secrete fructose-rich fluid for sperm nutrition.
Prostate Gland: Secretes alkaline fluid to protect sperm.
Bulbourethral Glands: Secrete lubricating mucus.
Penis: Organ for sexual intercourse.

slides.title: Structure of Sperm
content: Head: Contains the nucleus (DNA) and an enzyme to penetrate the egg.
Midpiece: Contains many mitochondria for energy production.
Tail (Flagellum): Provides movement for swimming toward the egg.

slides.title: Parts of the Female Reproductive System
content: Ovaries: Produce eggs (ova) and hormones (estrogen, progesterone).
Oviducts (Fallopian Tubes): Transport eggs; site of fertilization.
Uterus: Hollow organ where the embryo implants and develops.
Cervix: Opening of the uterus into the vagina.
Vagina: Organ of intercourse and the birth canal.
Vulva: External genitalia.

slides.title: Ovulation
content: The process of releasing a mature egg from an ovary.
A woman is born with thousands of eggs.
During her fertile years, only 300-400 eggs mature.
Occurs approximately once every 28 days.
The egg is released into the oviduct.

slides.title: The Menstrual Cycle
content: A monthly series of changes in the female reproductive system.
The average cycle is about 28 days.
It is controlled by hormones: FSH, LH, estrogen, and progesterone.
It prepares the uterus for a potential pregnancy.

slides.title: Phases of the Menstrual Cycle
content: 1. Flow Phase (Menstruation): Shedding of the uterine lining. Day 1-5.
2. Follicular Phase: FSH stimulates a follicle to mature; uterus lining thickens. Day 6-14.
3. Ovulation: LH surge triggers release of a mature egg from the ovary. Day 14.
4. Luteal Phase: Corpus luteum produces progesterone to prepare for pregnancy. Day 15-28.
If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum breaks down, and the cycle repeats.

slides.title: Menstrual Hygiene
content: Wear lightweight, breathable clothing.
Change menstrual products regularly to prevent infection.
Wash the external genital area daily with water only.
Use unscented products.
Drink enough water.
Track your period as a health marker.
Visit a healthcare provider for annual check-ups.

slides.title: Fertilization
content: The fusion of a sperm nucleus and an egg nucleus.
Occurs in the oviduct (Fallopian tube).
The resulting single cell is called a zygote.
The zygote is a unique combination of genetic material from both parents.

slides.title: Pregnancy and Development
content: The zygote undergoes cell division as it travels down the oviduct.
It forms a solid ball of cells (morula), then a blastocyst.
Implantation: The blastocyst embeds itself into the uterine lining.
The embryo is surrounded by amniotic fluid for protection.
The placenta develops to exchange nutrients, gases, and waste between mother and fetus.

slides.title: Twins
content: Identical (Monozygotic) Twins: From one fertilized egg that splits into two.
Fraternal (Dizygotic) Twins: From two separate eggs fertilized by two different sperm.

slides.title: Natural Methods
content: Abstinence: Avoiding sexual intercourse.
Fertility Awareness (Rhythm Method): Avoiding sex during ovulation by tracking the menstrual cycle, temperature, and cervical mucus.
Withdrawal (Coitus Interruptus): Pulling the penis out before ejaculation.

slides.title: Artificial Methods: Barrier
content: Male Condom: Latex sheath on the penis; prevents sperm from entering the vagina; protects against STIs.
Female Condom: Polyurethane sheath in the vagina; protects against STIs.
Diaphragm: Dome-shaped rubber disk covering the cervix; used with spermicide.
Spermicides: Chemicals that kill sperm; used with other barrier methods.

slides.title: Artificial Methods: Hormonal and Surgical
content: Contraceptive Pill: Daily pill with hormones to prevent ovulation.
Contraceptive Implant: Small tube under the skin that slowly releases hormones.
Contraceptive Injection: Hormone injection effective for 8-12 weeks.
Intrauterine Device (IUD): Small device inserted into the uterus to prevent implantation.
Vasectomy: Male sterilization by cutting the vas deferens.
Laparotomy (Tubal Ligation): Female sterilization by blocking the oviducts.

sections.section_title: 4.11 Sexually transmitted infections (STIs): Transmission and prevention

slides.title: Common STIs in Ethiopia
content: Trichomoniasis: Caused by a protozoan (Trichomonas vaginalis).
Chlamydia: Caused by bacteria (Chlamydia trachomatis).
Gonorrhea: Caused by bacteria (Neisseria gonorrhoeae).
Syphilis: Caused by bacteria (Treponema pallidum).
HIV/AIDS: Caused by a virus (Human Immunodeficiency Virus).

slides.title: Transmission of STIs
content: STIs are primarily transmitted through sexual contact.
They can also be transmitted through blood transfusions, sharing needles, and from mother to child during childbirth or breast milk.
Many STIs may not show early symptoms, which allows for their spread.

slides.title: Prevention and Control of STIs
content: Abstinence is the most effective method of prevention.
Using condoms (male and female) significantly reduces the risk of transmission.
Being faithful to one partner reduces risk.
Bacterial STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) are treatable with antibiotics.
Viral STIs (HIV/AIDS) have no cure, but medications can manage the disease and prolong life.

slides.title: Definition and Importance of Food
content: Food is any beneficial substance consumed to provide nutritional support.
Its importance includes:
Energy: Fuels all biological activities.
Growth: Provides substances for making new cells and tissues.
Repair: Replaces damaged tissues.
Protection: Prevents deficiency diseases.

slides.title: What is Nutrition?
content: Nutrition is the process of taking in food and converting it into energy and other vital nutrients.
It is the overall process by which an organism obtains and uses food.
Good nutrition is fundamental for survival, health, growth, and proper functioning of the body.

slides.title: Classes of Nutrients
content: 1. Carbohydrates: Provide energy (16 kJ/g).
2. Lipids (Fats and Oils): Provide concentrated energy (37 kJ/g), insulation, and vitamin absorption.
3. Proteins: Needed for growth and repair (17 kJ/g).
4. Vitamins: Regulate body processes (micronutrients).
5. Minerals: Essential for various body functions (micronutrients).
6. Water: Essential for all life processes.
7. Fiber (Roughage): Indigestible; prevents constipation.

slides.title: Carbohydrates: Sources and Function
content: Sources: Starch (potatoes, bread, rice, maize), sugars (fruits, sugarcane, honey).
Energy source for the body.
Provides dietary fiber (cellulose) to prevent constipation and maintain colon health.
Monosaccharides: Simple sugars (glucose, fructose, galactose).
Disaccharides: Two sugars linked (sucrose, lactose).
Polysaccharides: Many sugars linked (starch, glycogen, cellulose).

slides.title: Lipids: Sources and Function
content: Sources: Fats (animal sources, butter, cheese), Oils (plant sources, sunflower seeds, fruits).
High-energy nutrient.
Insulates the body against heat loss.
Serves as a vehicle for fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

slides.title: Proteins: Sources and Function
content: Sources: Animal (meat, fish, eggs, milk), Plant (beans, chickpeas, soy, nuts).
Essential for growth, tissue repair, and making enzymes, hormones, and cell structures.

slides.title: Vitamins: Types and Functions
content: Vitamin A: Good vision, healthy skin, and mucous membranes.
Vitamin B (Complex): Help with energy release and nervous system function.
Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid): Tissue repair, immune function, and wound healing.
Vitamin D: Absorption of calcium and phosphorus for strong bones and teeth.
Vitamin E: Protects cells from damage.
Vitamin K: Essential for blood clotting.

slides.title: Minerals: Types and Functions
content: Calcium: Bone and teeth formation, muscle and nerve function.
Iron: Formation of hemoglobin in red blood cells for oxygen transport.
Iodine: Production of thyroid hormones (regulates metabolism).
Phosphorus: Bone and teeth formation, energy storage and use.
Sodium and Potassium: Nerve signal transmission and fluid balance.

slides.title: What is a Balanced Diet?
content: A diet that contains all the nutrients in the correct amount and proportion.
Includes adequate carbohydrates and fats for energy.
Includes enough protein of the right kind for growth and repair.
Contains vitamins, minerals, fiber, and water.

slides.title: Nutritional Needs for Different Groups
content: Children: Need more energy and protein for growth.
Pregnant/Lactating Women: Increased nutritional needs for fetal development and milk production.
Elderly: Generally lower energy and protein needs, but a balanced diet is still crucial.
Athletes: High energy and protein requirements for muscle development and performance.
Men vs. Women: Men usually need more energy due to higher muscle mass.

slides.title: Common Deficiency Diseases
content: Kwashiorkor: Protein deficiency; symptoms: swelling of abdomen and legs, dry/flaky skin.
Marasmus: Energy deficiency; symptoms: extreme thinness, muscle wasting, old-looking face.
Anemia: Iron deficiency; symptoms: weakness, tiredness, irritability.
Rickets: Vitamin D deficiency; symptoms: soft, deformed bones.
Scurvy: Vitamin C deficiency; symptoms: bleeding gums, poor wound healing.

slides.title: What is Malnutrition?
content: Malnutrition is the insufficient, excessive, or imbalanced consumption of nutrients.
It includes both undernutrition and overnutrition.
Causes: Poverty, famine, disease, lack of nutritional knowledge.

slides.title: Undernutrition and Overnutrition
content: Undernutrition: Wasting (low weight for height), Stunting (low height for age), Underweight (low weight for age), Micronutrient deficiencies.
Overnutrition: Obesity, which is caused by an energy imbalance.
Obesity is a risk factor for heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, and arthritis.

slides.title: Body Mass Index (BMI)
content: BMI = Body mass (kg) / Height² (m²).
BMI Categories:
Underweight: < 18.5
Overweight: 25.0 - 29.9
Obese: ≥ 30.0
BMI is a useful guide, but it does not account for muscle mass.

slides.title: What is Substance Abuse?
content: Substance abuse is using legal or illegal drugs in the wrong way or in excess.
Legal substances that can be abused: Tobacco (nicotine), Alcohol, Khat.
Illegal drugs: Heroin, Cannabis.
Doping: Use of prohibited substances in sports.

slides.title: Effects of Tobacco Smoke: Tar
content: Tar is a black, sticky substance in cigarette smoke.
Effects on the respiratory system:
Chronic Bronchitis: Irritates and damages airways, causing excess mucus and narrowing.
Emphysema: Destroys alveoli, reducing oxygen absorption.
Lung Cancer: Contains carcinogens (cancer-causing agents).

slides.title: Effects of Tobacco Smoke: Carbon Monoxide and Nicotine
content: Carbon Monoxide: A poisonous gas that irreversibly binds to hemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport.
Effect: Increases risk of heart disease and stroke.
Nicotine: A stimulant and addictive substance.
Effect: Increases heart rate and blood pressure; narrows blood vessels.

slides.title: Effects of Drinking Alcohol
content: Alcohol is a depressant that slows down the brain and nervous system.
Short-term effects: Loss of coordination, loss of judgment, slower reaction times.
Long-term effects: Liver cirrhosis (scarring of liver tissue), stomach ulcers, heart disease, brain damage.

slides.title: Other Substances: Khat, Cannabis, Heroin
content: Khat: Contains cathinone; a stimulant causing alertness, but can lead to depression, sleep disorders, gastritis, and social problems.
Cannabis: Contains THC; a psychoactive drug affecting perception and memory; mental health risks.
Heroin: A powerful depressant; highly addictive; risk of overdose and infection from needle sharing.

slides.title: Doping in Sports
content: Doping is the use of prohibited substances to gain an unfair advantage in sports.
Banned classes: Anabolic steroids, stimulants, peptide hormones, blood doping.
Health risks: Cardiovascular, central nervous system, hormonal, and psychological side effects.
Consequences: Suspension, loss of medals, financial penalties, legal issues.

slides.title: Infectious Diseases: Transmission
content: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa, fungi).
Transmission methods:
Airborne (droplets from coughs/sneezes).
Direct contact (body fluids).
Contaminated food or water (fecal-oral).
Vector-borne (e.g., mosquitoes).
Sexual contact.

slides.title: Prevention of Infectious Diseases
content: Vaccination: Builds immunity against specific pathogens.
Personal hygiene: Handwashing, covering coughs.
Hygienic food preparation: Washing, cooking thoroughly.
Boiling drinking water: Kills pathogens.
Proper waste disposal: Prevents breeding of vectors.
Using condoms: Reduces risk of STIs.

slides.title: HIV/AIDS
content: Caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV).
HIV attacks and destroys T-lymphocytes (immune cells).
As T-cells decrease, the body becomes susceptible to opportunistic infections.
AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome) is the late stage of HIV infection.
Transmission: Sexual contact, blood transfusions, shared needles, mother to child.
Prevention: Abstinence, condoms, sterile needles, antiretroviral drugs during pregnancy.

slides.title: Tuberculosis (TB)
content: Caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Spread through airborne droplets when infected people cough or sneeze.
Symptoms: Persistent cough, chest pain, fever, weight loss.
Prevention: BCG vaccine, avoiding overcrowding, covering mouth when coughing.
Treatment: Long-term antibiotic therapy; drug resistance is a growing concern.

slides.title: Malaria
content: Caused by a protozoan parasite (Plasmodium).
Transmitted by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.
Control methods:
Reducing mosquito populations (eliminate breeding sites).
Preventing bites (insect nets, repellents).
Using antimalarial drugs (e.g., Artemisinin-based therapies).

slides.title: COVID-19
content: Caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus.
Spread through respiratory droplets from coughs, sneezes, and talking.
Symptoms: Fever, cough, fatigue, loss of taste or smell.
Prevention: Social distancing, mask-wearing, frequent handwashing, vaccination.

slides.title: Non-Infectious Diseases
content: Diseases not caused by pathogens.
Causes: Genetics, lifestyle factors, malnutrition, environmental factors.
Examples: Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency), Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), Lung cancer (smoking), Diabetes, Cardiovascular disease, Sickle cell anemia.

slides.title: Ethiopian Nutritionists
content: Nutritionists are researchers who study nutrition and its impact on health.
Their work is vital for addressing malnutrition and food insecurity in Ethiopia.
Through research and policy advice, they contribute to improving public health.

slides.title: What is Ecology?
content: Ecology is the branch of biology that studies the interactions among organisms and with their environment.
Scientists who study ecology are called ecologists.
They study the relationships between living things (biotic factors) and their non-living environment (abiotic factors).

slides.title: Key Ecological Concepts
content: Ecosystem: A community of organisms and their physical environment.
Habitat: The place where an organism lives.
Niche: The role or job an organism plays in its ecosystem (what it eats, where it lives, etc.).
Ecologists use both qualitative observations and quantitative measurements.

slides.title: Abiotic Factors
content: Abiotic factors are non-living components of the ecosystem.
Examples:
Solar energy: Powers most ecosystems.
Temperature: Affects metabolism and distribution of organisms.
Water: Essential for all life; availability limits distribution.
Nutrients: Like nitrogen and phosphorus, vital for plant growth.
Salinity: Salt concentration in aquatic environments.
Oxygen: Critical for aquatic organisms.

slides.title: Biotic Factors
content: Biotic factors are the living components of an ecosystem.
Examples:
Predators: Organisms that kill and eat prey.
Herbivores: Animals that eat plants.
Parasites: Organisms that live on or in a host and harm it.
Competition: Organisms competing for the same resource.
Pathogens: Disease-causing organisms.

slides.title: Levels of Ecological Organization
content: Organism: An individual living thing.
Population: A group of the same species in the same area.
Community: All the different populations in an area.
Ecosystem: The community plus its abiotic environment.
Biosphere: The sum of all ecosystems on Earth.

slides.title: What is an Ecosystem?
content: An ecosystem is a self-supporting unit of a community and its abiotic environment.
Energy flows through an ecosystem (from the sun to producers to consumers).
Matter is recycled within an ecosystem.

slides.title: Types of Ecosystems
content: Terrestrial Ecosystems (on land):
Forests, grasslands, deserts, tundra.
Aquatic Ecosystems (in water):
Freshwater: Lakes, ponds, rivers, streams.
Marine: Oceans, coral reefs, estuaries.

slides.title: What is a Biome?
content: A biome is a large geographic area characterized by its vegetation (terrestrial) or physical environment (aquatic).
They are classified by climate, especially temperature and precipitation.
The same biome can occur in different locations with similar climates.

slides.title: Major Terrestrial Biomes (Part 1)
content: Tropical Rainforest: Near equator, high rainfall, high biodiversity.
Desert: Very low rainfall, extreme temperatures, water-conserving species.
Savanna: Grassland with scattered trees, seasonal rainfall, large herbivores.
Temperate Grassland (Prairie): Seasonal temperature extremes, fertile soil.

slides.title: Major Terrestrial Biomes (Part 2)
content: Temperate Broadleaf Forest: Deciduous trees, moderate climate.
Boreal Forest (Taiga): Cold, coniferous forest.
Tundra: Extremely cold, permafrost, low-growing vegetation.

slides.title: Major Aquatic Biomes
content: Freshwater Biomes: Lakes, streams, rivers, wetlands.
Marine Biomes: Oceans, intertidal zones, coral reefs, estuaries.
Photic Zone: Zone with sufficient light for photosynthesis.
Aphotic Zone: Zone with little to no light.

slides.title: What is Ecological Succession?
content: Succession is the orderly, natural change in the composition of communities over time.
It is a process of gradual replacement of species.

slides.title: Primary Succession
content: Starts in a virtually lifeless area with no soil (e.g., new volcanic island, retreating glacier).
Pioneer species (lichens, mosses) are the first to colonize.
They break down rock, creating soil.
Over time, grasses, shrubs, and trees replace the pioneers.
Eventually leads to a stable climax community.

slides.title: Secondary Succession
content: Occurs after a major disturbance that removes most but not all of the community.
The soil remains intact.
Example: After a forest fire or clearing for agriculture.
Pioneer species are fast-growing weeds and grasses.
This process is faster than primary succession and eventually reaches a climax community.

slides.title: Types of Ecological Interactions
content: Competition (-/-): Both species are harmed.
Predation (+/-): One species benefits (predator), the other is harmed (prey).
Herbivory (+/-): One species benefits (herbivore), the other is harmed (plant).
Parasitism (+/-): Parasite benefits, host is harmed.
Mutualism (+/+): Both species benefit.
Commensalism (+/0): One species benefits, the other is unaffected.

slides.title: Competition and Predation
content: Competition: Interaction where individuals of different species use the same resource.
Examples: Weeds competing with garden plants; lions competing for prey.
Predation: Interaction where one species (predator) kills and eats another (prey).
Examples: Lion eating a zebra; rotifer eating a protist.

slides.title: Herbivory and Parasitism
content: Herbivory: An organism (herbivore) eats parts of a plant or alga.
Examples: Goats eating grass; caterpillars eating leaves.
Parasitism: One organism (parasite) derives nourishment from another (host), harming it.
Examples: Tapeworm in the intestine; tick on a dog.

slides.title: Mutualism and Commensalism
content: Mutualism: Interaction that benefits both species.
Examples: Pollination (bees and flowers); Mycorrhizae (fungi and plant roots).
Commensalism: Interaction that benefits one species and does not harm or help the other.
Examples: Cattle egrets following grazing animals to eat insects.
